text: If you think Formula One started in nineteen fifty, you're missing the fifty-six years that explain everything you see on the grid today.

A few years earlier, this place trained bomber crews for the Second World War. Now, on the thirteenth of May, nineteen fifty, its old perimeter roads have become a racetrack, lined with oil drums and straw bales, and a crowd of around a hundred thousand people has come to watch. Even the King and Queen are here: the only time a reigning British monarch has ever attended a motor race in Britain.

At the front of the grid sit four blood-red Alfa Romeos. Ferrari didn't even turn up, after a row over starting money. Seventy laps later, an Italian named Giuseppe Farina takes the chequered flag, and without quite realising it, everyone here has just watched the very first race of the Formula One World Championship. But that championship didn't appear out of nowhere. It was the answer to fifty-six years of problems, and the first one began with a newspaper trying to sell more newspapers.

In eighteen ninety-four, the car is barely ten years old. It's loud, it breaks down constantly, and most people think it's a toy for rich eccentrics. So the Paris newspaper Le Petit Journal announces a challenge: drive from Paris to Rouen, about a hundred and twenty-six kilometres, and prove these machines are actually useful. More than a hundred entries are sent in, but only twenty-one machines actually make it to the start.

And it isn't really a race. The judges are looking for a vehicle that is safe, easy to handle and cheap to run. So when Count de Dion's big steam tractor arrives first, it doesn't get the top prize, because it needs a second man on board just to stoke the boiler. That goes, shared, to two petrol car makers: Peugeot and Panhard. A year later, the stakes go up: Paris to Bordeaux and back again, almost twelve hundred kilometres. Emile Levassor drives through two nights, almost without rest, and gets back first after nearly forty-nine hours. But there's a catch. The rules say the winner must be a four-seat car, and Levassor's has only two. So the official victory goes to a Peugeot that arrives hours later.

Still, the point is made. A car that survives twelve hundred kilometres sells itself. Racing has become the best advertisement in the world, and that is the first reason Formula One exists: to prove the machine works.

The trouble is, the machines get fast much quicker than the roads get safe. By nineteen oh three, the biggest cars can top a hundred kilometres per hour, on dirt roads, through villages, with crowds standing right at the edge. That May, more than two hundred cars set off from Versailles, just outside Paris, heading for Madrid. The dust is so thick drivers can barely see the road, and spectators keep stepping out to get a closer look.

Crash follows crash. Among those killed is Marcel Renault, one of the three brothers who founded Renault. Trying to pass a rival in the dust, he misses a bend and hits a tree. His brother Louis reaches Bordeaux first in his class, and learns there what has happened. That night the French government stops the race. The cars aren't even allowed to start their engines again: horses tow them to the railway station.
That is the end of racing between cities on open roads. From now on, racing moves onto closed circuits: loops of road shut to the public. Reason number two: racing needs its own safe place.

Around the same time, the American newspaper owner James Gordon Bennett creates a cup for teams representing whole countries, not just car makers. To tell them apart, each nation is given a colour: blue for France, white for Germany, yellow for Belgium, and red for the United States. Britain can't use red, white or blue, because they're taken. And in nineteen oh three, Britain's home race has to be held in Ireland, because racing on public roads is illegal in Britain itself. So the British team goes green, and the story goes it was a nod to Ireland's shamrock. That's British racing green. Italy, which first raced in black, ends up with red a little later, and that's why, more than a century on, Ferrari still races in red.

In nineteen oh six, the Automobile Club of France runs a new kind of race on closed public roads near Le Mans, and gives it a grand name: the Grand Prix, French for big prize. Each lap is more than a hundred kilometres. The race runs over two days, twelve laps, more than twelve hundred kilometres in summer heat. In that heat, the roads break up and tyres explode. Changing one means cutting the old tyre off the wheel by hand, which can take well over ten minutes.

But Renault, like Fiat, has a new secret weapon: detachable rims from Michelin. Instead of cutting the tyre off, the crew swaps the whole rim in a couple of minutes. Their driver, a Hungarian mechanic named Ferenc Sis, wins at an average of about a hundred and one kilometres per hour, on dirt roads, in nineteen oh six. Grand Prix racing is born. But it is still a patchwork: every race has its own rules, and nobody is crowned champion of all of them.

In the nineteen thirties, Grand Prix racing finally gets a European Championship, and it also gets political. The German government backs two teams, Mercedes-Benz and Auto Union, to show off German engineering, and their silver cars, the Silver Arrows, become almost unbeatable. Legend says Mercedes scraped the white paint off their car to get it under the weight limit. It's a great story, but historians think it's probably made up: that weight limit wasn't even used at the race in question.

And they can be beaten. At the nineteen thirty-five German Grand Prix, in front of around three hundred thousand spectators, Tazio Nuvolari, in an outdated red Alfa Romeo, chases down the Silver Arrows and wins on the last lap. Then the Second World War stops everything. In Italy, Alfa Romeo has a small, brilliant racing car called the one fifty-eight. To keep it safe, the cars are hidden near Milan, in a cheese factory according to legend, on a pig farm according to others. Remember that car.

After the war, the sport's governing body, today called the FIA, writes one rulebook for top-level racing: a single formula. That's literally what the name means: a formula is the set of rules every car must follow, from engine size to weight. The first one allows either a big four point five litre engine, or a small one point five litre engine with a supercharger. Without it, the richest team simply builds the biggest monster. With it, very different machines can race on roughly equal terms. Reason number three: make it fair.

One thing is still missing. In nineteen forty-nine, motorcycles get their own world championship, and car racing doesn't want to be left behind. So in early nineteen fifty, according to most accounts, the Italian count Antonio Brivio proposes linking the big national Grands Prix into one season, with points for the top five finishers and one extra point for the fastest lap. The first season has seven races: six in Europe, plus the Indianapolis five hundred in America, which counts, even though almost no European drivers go.

And the first race of all is Silverstone, on that May day in nineteen fifty, won by the very model that spent the war hidden on a farm: the Alfa Romeo one fifty-eight. The title goes down to the final race at Monza, where Farina's own team-mate, a young Argentinian called Juan Manuel Fangio, leads him by two points. Farina wins the race, and the championship, by three points. Giuseppe Farina becomes Formula One's first World Champion. Reason number four: crown one champion.

So, why does Formula One exist? Because people needed to prove their machines worked, find a safe place to race them, make the fight fair, and crown one champion. Seventy-six years later, it's still the same four reasons. Car makers still use Formula One to prove their technology, teams still fight over every line of the rulebook, and twenty-two drivers still chase one title. Not bad for a newspaper stunt. Next time: how this sport went from a deadly hobby to a billion-dollar machine. Subscribe, and I'll see you on the grid.
